T1: Consumers will adopt lawn and garden tractors because they view them as a practical, low‑cost solution for small‑garden chores, and the company can capture value by selling directly to homeowners through its existing dealer network. Who benefits: Homeowners with small gardens benefit from a cheap, multipurpose tool; Deere benefits by selling through its existing dealer network, avoiding new distribution channels.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers shift from manual tools to powered equipment when they perceive a clear time‑saving benefit and a price point that is affordable for occasional use.. How value is captured: Deere sells tractors directly to dealers at a wholesale price, then dealers sell them to consumers, earning a margin and building brand loyalty that can be leveraged for future purchases.. Assumptions: Small‑garden households have sufficient disposable income to purchase a lawn tractor.; Deere’s dealer network is capable of stocking and selling consumer‑grade tractors.; Consumers trust Deere’s engineering for residential use.. Predictions: If Deere introduces a consumer‑focused lawn tractor, dealer orders will increase relative to existing tractor lines.; Consumer surveys will show that small‑garden owners cite cost and convenience as primary purchase drivers.; Sales data will show higher unit volume in regions with higher small‑garden density..

T2: Consumers will adopt lawn and garden tractors because they view them as a status symbol and a status-enhancing purchase, and the company can capture value by positioning tractors as premium, lifestyle products sold through specialty dealers. Who benefits: Homeowners seeking to signal wealth and modern lifestyle; Deere benefits by commanding higher prices and building brand prestige that can be leveraged for future premium purchases.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers shift from functional tools to status items when they perceive that ownership signals social standing and modern living; they are willing to pay more for a product that signals success.. How value is captured: Deere sells tractors at premium prices to select dealers who emphasize lifestyle branding; dealers earn higher margins and can charge more for accessories, creating a differentiated revenue stream.. Assumptions: Small‑garden households have disposable income sufficient for premium purchases.; Deere’s existing dealer network can be trained to position tractors as lifestyle items.; Consumers associate Deere with quality and status.. Predictions: If Deere introduces a consumer‑focused lawn tractor with lifestyle branding, dealer orders will increase in segments where consumers value status.; Consumer surveys will show that a majority of buyers cite status or prestige as a primary purchase driver.; Sales will be concentrated in affluent demographics where disposable income is higher..

Both groups continue selling existing tractor lines. Track dealer orders for the new consumer tractor over 12 weeks.. Sample: 20 independent dealers across the United States, selected from the existing dealer network, with at least 10 having prior residential lawn equipment sales.. Measure: Number of orders placed for the new consumer tractor per dealer in Group A vs Group B.. Predictions: T1: Group A will generate at least 15% more orders than Group B because residential demand drives sales.; T2: Group B will generate at least 15% more orders than Group A because status motivation drives sales.. Decision rule: If Group A orders exceed Group B by ≥15%, conclude T1 is better supported. If Group B orders exceed Group A by ≥15%, conclude T2 is better supported. If the difference is <15%, both theories remain uncertain.. Cost: 15000 euros, 12 weeks.

Who benefits: Individual consumers seeking to signal participation in specific activities (e.g., music, outdoor recreation, industrial work) and Hellberg Safety through premium pricing and brand association.. Why behaviour changes: When consumers view hearing protection as a visible, status-enhancing accessory rather than a functional necessity, they are willing to buy multiple units for different contexts, increasing per-customer revenue.. How value is captured: Hellberg can capture value by offering limited-edition designs, customization options, and higher-margin accessories, while leveraging its existing distribution to reach individual buyers directly.. Assumptions: Consumers associate hearing protection with a specific activity or lifestyle.; Status signaling is a primary driver for purchase decisions.; Hellberg can design and market differentiated products without compromising core safety performance.. Predictions: Surveyed consumers will indicate intent to purchase multiple units for different activities.; Sales of differentiated products will correlate with activity participation rates.; Willingness-to-pay for a status-oriented version will exceed that for a generic version..

Who benefits: Individual consumers who must meet safety standards for work, outdoor activities, or regulated environments, and Hellberg Safety through premium safety-compliant products and compliance marketing.. Why behaviour changes: When compliance is mandatory or perceived risk is high, consumers prioritize safety-certified products and are willing to pay a premium for verified protection, even if they do not seek status signaling.. How value is captured: Hellberg can capture value by emphasizing safety certifications, offering compliance-focused marketing, and selling through B2B channels or safety-focused retailers, leveraging its existing safety reputation.. Assumptions: Regulatory or safety requirements exist for the targeted activities.; Consumers prioritize safety over status in purchase decisions for those activities.; Hellberg can maintain core safety performance while offering differentiated designs for compliance.. Predictions: Surveyed consumers will cite safety compliance as a primary purchase driver for targeted activities.; Sales of differentiated products will be higher in markets with strong safety regulations.; Compliance-focused marketing will increase purchase intent compared to status-focused messaging..

Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Status Group (message emphasizing lifestyle, status, and multiple-use design) or Safety Group (message emphasizing safety compliance, regulatory requirements, and single-use for a specific activity). Both groups view the same differentiated product concept (e.g., a. Sample: 500 adult consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and participation in targeted activities (e.g., music, outdoor recreation, industrial work).. Measure: Willingness-to-pay (WTP) for the differentiated product, measured on a 7-point scale (1 = would not pay at all, 7 = would pay the highest price). Secondary measure: purchase intent (binary: would buy).. Predictions: T1: Status Group will report a higher average WTP and higher purchase intent than Safety Group.; T2: Safety Group will report a higher average WTP and higher purchase intent than Status Group.. Decision rule: If Status Group’s average WTP ≥ €30 and ≥ 15 percentage points higher than Safety Group’s average WTP, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition focused on status signaling. If Safety Group’s average WTP ≥ €30 and ≥ 15 percentage points higher than Status Group’s average WTP, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition focused on safety compliance. If neither. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Who benefits: Consumers gain tailored protection for specific activities (e.g., outdoor recreation, industrial work, concerts).. Why behaviour changes: When a product is marketed as optimized for a particular activity, consumers perceive higher relevance and are willing to buy a specialized version rather than a generic one.. How value is captured: Hellberg can charge premium prices for activity-specific models and sell through specialty retailers targeting those activities, capturing higher margins per unit.. events.text: Objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence to justify ACR Electronics investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, based on public information available up to late 2002.. Constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.; Investment decision must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, market opportunity, or competitive advantage.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeframe for any proposed experiment.; Evidence must address the feasibility of reaching individual buyers and the value capture mechanism.; Alternatives must include no expansion (continuing current B2B focus) and options not suggested in the question.. Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual outdoor enthusiasts (e.g., hikers, campers, emergency preparedness kits) using the 406 MHz distress beacon.; 2) Expand into a new B2B segment (e.g., emergency response agencies, search and rescue teams) leveraging the same technology.; 3) No expansion: continue focusing on existing B2B markets (ships, aircraft, military, commercial marine) without new consumer proposition.; 4) License the 406 MHz distress‑beacon technology to third‑party manufacturers for consumer applications.; 5) Partner with outdoor retailers or emergency preparedness brands to co‑brand a consumer product based on ACR’s technology..
